game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Interactive story hidden behind a simple detective game [/h1]

While the game's premise sounds pretty interesting, the gameplay is quite simple. You read various things such as Internet pages (forums, bank account extract, company's webpage, etc), chat discussions,  listen to live calls which are transcribed and some parts of the text will be highlighted which you can then drag and drop to [b]Orwell[/b], a database which unlocks additional things if a link can be established with the information you've taken.
For a non-spoiler example: you search a person's personal blog and you can find and analyze their username which can then be linked to another forum where it's used for more juicy contents.

It's a bit like [u]A Lost Phone[/u] but its puzzles are MUCH simpler and you can't really get stuck for too long as there's plenty of helpful indicators. Actually, the best part of the game where I really concentrated was when the amount of datachunks (highlighted parts of data in texts) you could import was limited. This really made you think if a [strike]favorite color[/strike] hobby such as artist is a valuable piece of data or not (you could be redirected to an artist page showing past gigs/locations or a contact phone number!).

The best part of the game is the story, because in the end, there's a story and it's told little by little, there are some interesting plot parts (Sorry won't spoil anything) and even if the gameplay sounds boring, the pace is really good and I didn't see time pass by while I finished the 5 episodes. It takes a little bit more than one hour per episode, maybe faster if you just drag and drop without reading.
Even if having a [i]know it all[/i] tool, there are plenty of mysteries to uncover and discovering bit by bit the personalities and relationships of the people you [strike]spy on[/strike] is pretty addictive.

The presentation is pretty nice with its stylish interface. Graphics isn't the most important part of the game but it's good that it's pleasing to the eyes. The music does also its job, it changes when there's a [b]gasp[/b] moment. 

In summary, I recommend this game if you like simple but well told story in a different way than just watching Netflix. It has a nice conspiracy/detective vibe and getting to the finish is an entertaining (and bumpy) ride.
I have definitely put the season 2 on my wishlist!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A very interesting narrative experience that pulls you in quite well with busywork, much like Papers, Please. It has a very well-crafted and smooth user interface that could totally pass for a real spying program. The game gives you loads of freedom in how you selectively pass on information to alter the plot, and everything from what you choose to save to WHEN you choose to save it can affect the course of the story. At times, these flashpoints are signposted a little too hard, presumably to give players plenty of time to sort through the information at hand and come to a decision, but there are multiple instances when you have to make genunely DIFFICULT choices relying only on your intuition and the information you have gathered thus far. The game does not hold your hand about the consequences your actions will have.

However, the ending did feel a bit contrived and (while foreshadowed well enough), not terribly well justified. I know too well the amount of work that must have gone into such an involved branching story, but the game felt too short. Just when it was beginning to get difficult and the amount of information you had to deal with started to grow burdensome, the game ends. It feels a bit rushed out the door, and doesn't give you enough of a chance to play with the mechanics and start to really sweat. Ultimately, this reveals the underlying issue with Orwell: It is not a game. It is a moral lesson wrapped in an interactive experience. The developers had something they wanted to say, and so the game must come to an end so that they can say it.

I completed the 5-day story in 3-4 hours, but it has some replayability in going back to explore alternate outcomes if you had taken different paths. However, this robs the game of its magic; because you're making difficult decisions based on limited info, a blind playthrough adds a considerable amount. On your second playthrough, you're really just going through the motions to see what happens, which makes the leisurely pace at which characters interact torturous and tends to expose the man behind the curtain when you see how your choices DON'T affect the story.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Personally, I'm loving this game so far. I'll most likely update the review after the next three episodes come out, but I don't believe my opinions will change all that drastically.

Orwell is a game where you investigate a crime (a bombing, to be precise) using the brand-new Orwell system, presumably named after famous author George Orwell, author of 1984. Using the program, you can identify data that might be necessary to your investigation, slowly collecting it and linking it together to form a case for your superior to take a look at and give his verdict.

Some data is useless; do you really need to know what this woman's favourite colour or food is? Is someone's address being "somewhere over the rainbow" on one of their social networking profiles pertinent information to the case? No, and adding too much useless data can cloud the system, leading to the wrong conclusion by your supervisor at the end. One of my personal favourites was having someone logged in on someone else's account mention their profession, and it came up as data for the account's owner. Presumably, if in an online chat, you joked you killed a man, or were a descendant of King Arthur, that would show up in the Orwell system as important information.

Other data is in conflict; for example, if a Facebook timeline would have someone changing their relationship status to "in  a relationship with whoever", and then later changing it to "single", which one would be the correct data to input? You cannot remove data once you upload, so you have to think long and hard about which to use. Of course, in this example, you could look at whichever was more recent, but the decisions can be harder and more complicated than that, I promise you. I commend this game having pieces of in-conflict data show up as conflicted even if you haven't found the other data yet, so you can't choose A (the only option at the time) and then have option B, the secret correct answer, be revealed to you later.

You also have the ability to, once you have contact details (such as phone numbers, email addresses, etc.), access your target's phone calls, emails, chat histories. These play out in real time, but you can easily go back to searching through websites for info, and return once the conversation is done.

And I won't spoil anything, but the ending of the second episode had me almost falling off my seat in anticipation and anxiety, hoping my guesses weren't wrong. I punched the air and shouted "YES" pretty loudly when it was revealed I was correct. The game got me way more emotionally involved than I was expecting.

If the idea of this interests you, buy the game. It'll definitely be worth the money. If you're on the fence, never fear! There is a free demo which contains the first episode of five. You now have no reason not to go try it. Go try it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is a very interesting game, especially for anyone who has an interest in the surveillance state and the pros and cons of such a thing, mixed in with choices that really seem to matter.  I will admit that I have have, at the time of writing this review only played one playthrough, but the story was compelling and the information that I chose to put in/leave out really seemed to impact what was happening.  On top of that, the story is compelling, interesting and told through a very interesting way, feeding you snippets as you dig through the personal lives and media presence of several NPCs with various connections to one another, with a simple lock-off system that makes sense in-universe (we don't have clearance to investigate this person who has some connection to a potential suspect).

Beyond that, the only real issue I have with the game is the few interface bugs.  As the game went on, I found myself getting glitched to certain websites, mostly the [spoiler]work profile of the concerned one woman after she died in a shootout with law enforcement, and occasionally it would glitch to her dating profile.  This would normally happen when I was in either the listener or insider tools, seemingly never when I was on the reader tool already.  It would just switch me over as I tried to open a file on the insider, or load up into a machine, or even when I'd try opening a new conversation in the listener.[/spoiler]
One more slight drawback about the game is that sometimes you get told a bit too much by the game.  Game not letting you progress?  Something you thought was a lie was probably true.  Yellow highlight instead of blue?  You're going to get some information that conflicts with that.  I realise it would be a lot more work but a way to mark information as lies rather than just disabling it might help.  People don't always tell the truth and if you come to the conclusion that something true is a lie, it would be nice if the game didn't give away that you're wrong by just stopping time for you.  As for the other issue, it might be nice getting a window saying "Hey, this piece of information you're trying to add conflicts with this other information you've already added...which one do you think is true?", instead of just "Hey, at some point probably in the next 10 minutes you'll get another piece of information that will conflict with this here, we know that even though in-universe we haven't made the connection that that page with the conflicting information even exists!"

All in all a really great game with a simple premise, easy to learn with some fairly minor flaws that can honestly be overlooked most of the time.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b] Orwell [/b]

First of, the game "Orwell" is based on the worldwidly popular novel "1984" by George Orwell, whose surname was picked as the game title and which is set in a totalitarian surveillance state. The game is one of the few games that are being released these days that feature unique gameplay and new ideas, although it's not as popular as it would deserve to be. I, however, bought this game during a recent Steam Sale because it struck my eye and I was interested in this.

[h1] What is Orwell and how does it work you ask? [/h1]

Well, in general, "Orwell" is a game where you're supposed to stop crimes with the use of the new software called "Orwell" in a world that is set in our present. You were the chosen one for the new job as a government agent, alone and in charge of "Orwell". Your only direct communication is "Sykes", another agent speaking to you over a one-way-channel and evaluating your actions and decisions. At first, you're being introduced by a short cutscene about an incident that has just happened: a bombing. Now, your task as an anti-crime agent is to find out who committed the crime and later on arrest him or her. At first, you as the "Orwell"-Agent can observe target people (you start with one that was quite obvious in the opening) with the help of 3 programs: the Reader, something to browse news and websites with, the Listener, to eavesdrop on target people once you've collected their number, and finally the Insider, where you can actively browse through the target's personal computer, once again if you collected a certain data. At first you should be browsing through their "Timelines", a website that is similar to social media that we have, e.g. Facebook and Twitter, collecting basic information of them, something like their name, address, birth date and so on. These information are "datachunks" that you can upload to "Orwell" to fill out the targets profile, but you must be careful, as you will not be able to remove data once uploaded. You will get to know your target pretty fast pretty soon as you can observe everything they do online. Later on, there will be so-called "conflicting datachunks", which include at least 2 datachunks. If you choose one datachunk out of the conflicting pair and upload it, the other datachunk will be disabled, so you have to choose wisely once again. If you've done everything right and chose after your liking you will soon arrest your first suspect, great job! After successfully managing a day, you "log off" of "Orwell" and end your day, your work is over for today. As you progress through the episodes, you'll quickly realize how complicated your "first tutorial task" in your new job get and how everything is connected to each other, but I don't want to spoil all your fun.

"Orwell" features 5 episodes for one price in total, releasing 1 each week, and as of 11/11/2016, 4 episodes are already out.

[h1] Do I like it? [/h1]

I definitely do. It's not a very gameplay intensive game, but rather a point and click/drag game, with a bit of thinking involved, however, I think it's very relaxing and it features a packing story. Although, to fully understand the story you have to read everything you find, or you will only get half of the story, which is why I usually need around 90 mins for a full episode, decision making included. The game devs had a really great idea for a new video game and it's almost a bit frightening to decide, whether a person is guilty or not, only based on online data and the game also once again brings up the controversy about surveillance by the government, even in the most private sectors. I mean, you can read what they write to their closest friends and listen to their phone calls. Nonetheless, it's a very innovative game that I really enjoyed, also the soundtrack of the game fits the situation very well and overall, for a 10$ game, "Orwell" is a master piece. I really hope they release a second part of the game or more episodes.

I definitely RECOMMEND the game, and if you're still a bit unsure, you can still try the demo and see for yourself, before you make a decision.

review_text_raw:
Orwell is a short but very well executed mystery detective.

The game starts off with the player working as an investigator in a security program called Orwell which allows tracking of every step of every person in The Nation. What starts as a detective case of a terrorist attack with a single suspect quickly turns into series of endless leads and plot twists.

Although most of the game consists of reading text it wasn’t boring for a second. Player has all the information at the palm of their hands and yet not everything is relevant or even true which forces fact checking and making decisions about the information they use and provide to the case. It’s even possible to leave out crucial information if a player thinks it’s a right thing to do.  It’s hard to describe the experience without spoiling anything but the story, consequential choices, dilemmas, connections you make during your investigation and twists around every corner are impeccable and had me on the edge of my seat for the entire playthrough. 

This game is definitely not for everyone, hell, I didn’t even think I myself would like it, but if you’re into mysteries and detectives it’s a must play. I’m usually not a big fan of these type of games or indie games in general, but Orwell blew me away, it was a brilliant experience.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It's so easy to get invested in the lives of little people when you can instantly find info about them on the internet, posts they've made, read their E-Mails, listen in on their phone calls and violate privacy in other ways.

EDIT: I've decided to add some more on to this review, since I really do think this game is good, and it deserves a more detailed review than what I wrote.

There's one thing that I really want people to know about in this game. Other reviews will probably talk about everything else, but what really caught my attention is how well characterized this world they've created is.

The developers did a really good job at presenting not only the people, but also the issues the game touches on firmly and equally. In any other game, or even film or book, it would no doubt be written to make the Government a bunch of faceless, freedom hating cronies who only feel passion from taking away liberties from the people, and to portray the rebels as the uncompromising heroes of humanity and answer to every problem possible. Instead, the developers made both sides of the 'war' have their strengths and weaknesses in every interpretation of the term. For example: the Government you work for is clearly doing good things, and the Orwell program puts you in contact with Symes, a human handler, who is just like any other person in the game: he has a personality and a history in game, is very friendly to the player and is clearly passionate in his work for the Government. My point is, the developers do a really good job at making them seem like they're doing good, and even makes you sympathise with the good the Government is doing, despite some of the questionable things they do in game and the horrific implications of even having a program like Orwell in the works.

Meanwhile, the "rebel" group that you spend each episode investigating is full of young, flawed people who seem more like a disfunctional group of friends than any liable threat to national security. As you investigate each member, you come to understand their personalities and struggles, but (to me at least) never fully support what they're doing or why they are doing it.

This is what earned a recommendation from me.

TL;DR: The games is good because instead of taking the quick and easy path, they make both sides of the 'war' and in extension the argument realistic positives and negatives.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[i]Orwell[/i] is a text-based game that puts you in the shoes of a crowdsourced cybersurveillance data clerk.

So, in the late 2000s The Nation has been suffering from a spiralling crime rate and unstable neighbours. This propelled the notoriously authoritarian Party to power, who then passed the vague-named Safety Bill. Basically, The Nation is an Americanish country that is careening towards a police state: the Safety Bill allows the government unlimited remote access to any electronic device they can identify, and extended detentions without charge for even slightly unfortunate turns of phrase. They have bots that can sift through that data for those unfortunate phrases. However, knowing the kind of jinn they are letting out the bottle, they created the solution: ORWELL, and you. As the anonymous Investigator, a foreign citizen, you are to evaluate the “datachunks” the automated system highlights among the information on designated target persons. The police only see the datachunks you feed into the system, and will generally take them literally; they can send you texts, but that’s it. It’s up to you to balance nuance, ethics and expedience, and to choose what to submit and what not to submit.

This gives you quite a bit of liberty. You can be the zealous [i]chekist[/i], using your omnipotent tools to not crush bones but crush souls, helping the police ravage through people’s lives. You can be the manipulator, minimizing the collateral damage and keeping the often trigger-happy police from harming their own cause. Or you can go full rebel and do your best to sabotage the investigation.

Now, as a bombing kills several people, and an apparently radicalized anti-surveillance group seems to be behind it in a massive bout of irony, you are to put your Internet detective hat on, and validate the system in a trial by fire, and a race against the clock.

Beyond the sometimes counterintuitive plot twists, I’ve found no issues with the game.

You’ll probably like it if you liked [i]Papers, Please[/i].

The story is excellent. Just when you thought you got to the bottom of it, it pulls the rug under your feet and goes even deeper. Several times i was sure i deduced everything and solved the mystery, and every time new information appeared and made me completely rethink everything. By the end it forms a messy web, yet i could see through it a coherent story and everything made sense. The whole thing is just very immersive.
Here, like in many story driven games, the gameplay is just a tool to deliver the plot, and the only thing that really matters is if it does it well without being too distracting. This may be up to personal taste, but i found it enjoyable enough that i didn't feel bored at any moment. Reading through articles and text conversations looking for useful data and following the story was engaging. Though i suppose if you don't enjoy too much reading in games it might get monotonous inbetween the story segments.
Overall would recommend it, especially if you're looking for a good engaging story.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Play as an investigator in a new secret gov. program named 'Orwell' that -- unsurprisingly -- spies on its own citizens' e-mails, phone conversations, laptops, etc., and selectively hunts for evidence of unlawful activity. The focus in this 5-part story is anti-governmental terrorism.

The name Orwell is on the nose, of course, and the writing is mostly along those lines. (This game is all text, all writing, so this is very important!) It, however, begins unraveling near the end, reaching for genuine philosophical depth. A favorite moment that's a bit too prescient is at the end while digging through the (optional) files that led to Orwell's creation. One of the creators calls the program Orwellian in its sinister direction. It's meant as a pejorative. The other creators have no idea who Orwell is -- one of the most famous English writers of the 20th century, and most influential on pop culture for over 50 years. They just think Orwell is a cool name, and so they use it unironically to name their entire Orwellian program. 

Do you see what's neat here?

I went in thinking Orwell didn't exist in this game's universe. But he does. And he's still a huge influence. The fictional government is so ignorant, run by idiots hell-bent on imaginary terrorism and protecting themselves and their interests, though, that the messages of Orwell's books are lost on them -- and they just don't care. 

This should sound familiar. This game felt like a fluffy beach-read dystopia in 2016, but it quickly turned accurate once January 20th rolled around in 2017. Awesome.

review_text_raw:
It's a good looking game with a good narrative

This game is a slow burn. It reels you in with it's fun interface and somewhat casual atmosphere but sooner then later it takes a nose dive into high risks and seriously weird situations. The gameplay is slower, but I feel that the slower pace complements the narrative.

You operate as a investigator on a program called Orwell, intended to keep the citizens of the State safe. Things get heated after a bombing and you are off, looking for the culprit and connecting seemingly unrelated pieces. Do the ends justify the means?  

There are segments in the game where you have to listen to long-winded phone calls and I see that some did not like that aspect or would like to be able to fast forward in those parts, so just keep that in mind.


TL;DR:
'Tis a good game but slow at times. 
You get to fulfill your stalking fantasies.
10/10, plus the visuals are nice!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
9/10

Orwell is a surveillance game (I suppose you could call it). However, there is also a machine/program in the game called Orwell that gameplay centers around. 

The program seems to have two functions. The first is a tracking function: if the player provides a website, a chat handle, a phone number, an e-mail address, or even a computer ID (I suppose this is analogous to an IP address), the program will then "track" it. If a phone call comes in on the number, you can listen in. If a blog has an update, Orwell lets you know, etc. Often, you'll get a chat handle, then in the chat you'll find a phone number or e-mail, which you can then track. From all this data you can create profiles of persons of interest, which is the second function of the program. Through data, you can learn who knows who, and how they know each other.

Law Enforcement uses the information collected to locate and arrest those individuals that you've deemed possible suspects in crimes. The game begins with a bomb exploding in a public square. I won't give any more of the story away, because it's quite an interesting ride.

On the surface, this gameplay sounds straightforward, but there are juicy complications. For instance, if someone denounces the government harshly in a fit of rage after paying taxes, do they represent a danger to the government? If Orwell (the program) didn't have a human operator, could it read between the lines? To further increase the stakes, any data uploaded to Orwell is permanent. So I couldn't designate this hypothetical taxpayer as a threat and then clarify later that he didn't "mean" what he said.

Also, if someone was aware of the program, could they provide false meeting places to divert law enforcment? Do your persons of interest know that you know they know about Orwell? 

It's a very well done and thought-provoking game, especially in the age of big data. Not only does it explore some of the limitations of using data collection for crime prevention, but it makes the player realize just how much information about themselves they've made public online.

For instance, Judith Duportail (a writer for the Guardian) requested the data that the dating site Tinder had collected on her. In September 2017, she published an article detailing the experience. Tinder sent her 800 pages of material.

In this game you take the role of a CIA agent in 2012 using the tool that was leaked by Edward Snowden, XKeyScore. 

Your tasked with getting the guys responsible for 3 terrorist acts in jail. You quickly stumble upon a group called The Thot. Everyone in it is clearly a terrorist and should've been arrested decades ago. The whole game you are wondering what's taking your supervisor so long to finally arrest the fools. 

So i finally get to the end of act 5. I identified the 3 terrorists: Everyone in the thot group, the supervisor woman (Sykes was cool, the woman is clearly shady), and the owners of the pharmaceutical company. I couldn't get the supervisor arrested nor the pharmaceutical owners. But luckily everyone in thot was jailed. Good. Then for whatever reason they wanted me arrested. Not exactly clear why this happens since I did everything right, probably a game bug.

Overrall the game is pretty good. It walks the fine line between story and lack of gameplay (that's where you see the positive and negative reviews coming from). And for me it was more towards the good side of the line. I'd say it's worth it but not for 10 bucks. I got it in the humble bundle jumbo bundle.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]A must-play for any cyber-security enthusiast[/h1]

[i]Received this as a gift from a dear friend[/i]

[b]Note:[/b]

Playing this game involves a lot of reading and if that's not your thing, you're probably not gonna enjoy Orwell.
But if you like playing VN's, I believe you'll love it!

[b]Gameplay:[/b]

You're an investigator in a secret mass-surveillance program run by the government, called Orwell (named after [url=https://youtu.be/h9JIKngJnCU]George Orwell, author of the novel '1984'[/url]).
Your job is to read up the information in your [i]Reader[/i] and upload [i]chunks[/i] of it to the Orwell database.
Uploading certain information may open up more leads and you may get unrestricted access to the 'target' person's PC, mobile, medical records and what not.

At certain times, you may find conflicting bits of information.
At such times, it's best to avoid resolving the issue. Read other relevant details and when you come back, it'd be clear to you what the right information is.

During the entire course of the game, all you do is read - a person's social network feed, their blogs. Sometimes you tap their calls and messages. But, you never directly interact with the individuals.
Yet, you gain so much knowledge about them that you practically know the person. Without actually [i]knowing[/i] them.
And all that just in the timeframe of 5 days!
It's kinda amazing and disturbing at the same time.

Also, the most important thing. Once an information is uploaded to Orwell, it cannot be deleted.
And there could be consequences depending on what you upload.
So, you wanna be careful, to not wrongly accuse an innocent. Which, trust me, is not that easy.

[b]My thoughts:[/b]
[i](May contain SPOILERS. Or it may simply affect your experience of the game. So read at your own risk ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ )[/i]

I loved the game.
Government mass surveillance has been a topic of concern for quite some time now.
It was ingenious to make a game that puts the player on the opposite side of the coin where the player is the one carrying out the surveillance.

At first, while it's all new and sunny, you feel like an unrivaled God - passing righteous judgments, punishing the wrong-doers. That is what you're made to believe you are.
And you find all sorts of crazy, unstable people in the world that you feel they [i]need[/i] to be surveilled.
Then you find out that they had a disturbing past that made them into what they are.
Then you realize that passing righteous judgments is a lot more difficult than you had initially assumed. And that personal data is a sensitive thing and it can destroy lives. And that YOU might be destroying someone's life as a part of your [i]work[/i].
If you're lucky, you'll wake up in time and realize how faulty the system is. And how you've been probing into other's personal lives and just how despicable that really is.
Otherwise, you either lose your humanity forever and become a Dementor that feeds on other people's personal lives. Or you go insane. Or both.

Maybe this journey of realization is similar to the one Edward Snowden had. Only, his journey was real and his actions had real consequences.
I would strongly recommend anyone to watch [url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt3774114/]Snowden[/url] and [url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt4044364/]Citizenfour[/url] after playing the game if you haven't already.

review_text_raw:
Orwell is a visual novel kind of game that gives you the tools to snoop into people's bank accounts, computers, private conversations and social media sites. You will have to decide which pieces of information are relevant and whether you will reveal your subject's most intimate secrets to the government surveillance program. You gradually build networks and figure out various connections.

I really like the style and feel of the game. It's easy to think that Orwell gives you the opportunity to play the bad guy who merely rats out people who try to change the world for better, but in the end it's hard to point fingers. Orwell is not black and white. 

The game is not very hard. The graphics are clean and simple, and the writing is very immersive and every now and there's a gripping sense of urgency. In a funny way I also grew attached to these people I was surveilling and exposing. It's entertaining and good food for thought.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Now, when I went into Orwell, I was fairly certain of what I would be getting out of my experience. An interesting little narrative set in an Orwellian-universe where you help figure out who perpetrated a terrorist attack. In a way, that's exactly what I got. But, looking back on my time with the game, I'm struck by how utterly wrong I was. Orwell exceeds all expectations and leaves me itching to either give the game another go, or threaten the developers at knife point to let me play Season 2, which the game helpfully reminded me to add to my wishlist before exiting the program.

I'm sure there's some connection that can be made to the game monitoring me in that last sentence, but I'll let it slide because Orwell deserves all the levity I can grant it.

Addressing the actual game instead of gushing all over my laptop and nearby furniture, it plays out as a sort of Point-and-Click adventure game where websites, conversations, and remote connections act as different areas, and datablocks act as items. The real twist is that, once you collect a new piece of information, there is no undo button. Your supervisor can only see what you let him see, and you can't take any information back if you realize you made a bad call or acted too hastily. And the game makes you live with it. After making a particularly blatant error, I fell back into bad habbits and attempted to quit the game and allow myself another go from whatever autosave the game keeps. 

Unfortunately for my inner gaming sins, Orwell knows exactly where you left off, as the exit screen likes to remind you. If you mess up, you've messed up permanently on that file. Wanna redo? Looks like you're starting over.

This knowledge that everything you do will have intentional and unintentional consequences makes this the most tense and nerve wracking narrative experience i've played in quite some time. This is especially apparent in the final act, which I won't be spoiling because everyone needs to experience the game's final twists and turns for themselves.

As much as I love the game, it isn't entirely without flaws. Some of the indicators for new information disappear too quickly, forcing me to search through articles trying to locate missing data. There are times where the information you need to use to progress the investigation is incredibly obscure, sending you on another hidden picture adventure. And, while I love the eavesdropping system, it can be somewhat tiresome to watch a conversation playout when you're dead set into 'Network Super Sleuth' mode and have to wait for dialogue to end before resuming the hunt. 

But all of those are nitpicks. The game is fantastic, and it makes me long for more games with this style of narrative/gameplay interaction. While I won't be playing through until I thoroughly forget some of the game's twists, rest assured I will be delving back into the world of The Party in the future.

As much as I love the game, it isn't entirely without flaws. Some of the indicators for new information disappear too quickly, forcing me to search through articles trying to locate missing data. There are times where the information you need to use to progress the investigation is incredibly obscure, sending you on another hidden picture adventure. And, while I love the eavesdropping system, it can be somewhat tiresome to watch a conversation playout when you're dead set into 'Network Super Sleuth' mode and have to wait for dialogue to end before resuming the hunt. But all of those are nitpicks. The game is fantastic, and it makes me long for more games with this style of narrative/gameplay interaction. While I won't be playing through until I thoroughly forget some of the game's twists, rest assured I will be delving back into the world of The Party in the future.
